summary.text: Flowering plants, or angiosperms, bear flowers and fruits, and their seeds are enclosed within a fruit.
They are by far the most diverse group of land plants, with approximately 300,000 known species.
Agriculture depends almost entirely on them, and rice, maize and wheat alone provide half of the world's staple calories.

items.prompt: Biologists named this plant group from Greek words for 'container' and 'seed'. What does the name describe?

options.label: The plant carries its seeds in cones
The seeds sit enclosed within a fruit
The plant stores seeds in its roots
The plant drops its seeds into water

items.explain: Angiosperm comes from Greek words meaning container and seed, meaning that the seeds are enclosed within a fruit.

items.prompt: A botanist finds a seed plant whose xylem is made of vessel elements and whose fruits completely wrap the seeds. Which group is it?

options.label: A fern, which spreads by spores

items.explain: Angiosperms differ from gymnosperms by having flowers, vessel-element xylem, endosperm and fruits that envelop the seeds.

items.prompt: A garden has deep, tube-shaped blooms. Which visitor has the flower most likely evolved to suit?

options.label: Wind carrying pollen from tree to tree
A crawling beetle with short mouthparts

items.explain: Tube-shaped flowers often coevolve with long-tongued insects or hummingbirds, while gymnosperms rely mainly on wind.

items.prompt: Two populations of one wildflower slowly grow blooms shaped for different pollinators. What may that eventually lead to?

options.label: The two populations merging into one

items.explain: Small changes in floral structure can shift a plant's pollinator reliance, driving reproductive isolation and new species.

items.prompt: On land, flowering plants dominate almost everywhere. A hiker looks for an exception among four places. Which one is it?
items.explain: On land, flowering plants are the dominant plant group in every habitat except frigid moss-lichen tundra and coniferous forest.

items.prompt: A plant lives in poor, acidic bog soil and traps insects. What does it gain from them?

options.label: Nutrients such as nitrate that the soil lacks
Seeds to carry to other bogs

items.explain: Sundews in nutrient-poor acid bogs are carnivorous and derive nutrients such as nitrate from trapped insects.

paragraphs.heading: Plants that make flowers
paragraphs.text: Flowering plants are the plants that produce flowers and fruits. Biologists call them angiosperms, a name built from Greek words for a container and a seed, pointing to seeds held inside a fruit. They are land plants with roots, stems, leaves and seeds, just as gymnosperms are. The group takes in every forb, which is a flowering plant with no woody stem, plus grasses, most broad-leaved trees, shrubs and vines, and most water plants.

paragraphs.heading: Set apart from gymnosperms
paragraphs.text: Gymnosperms are the other main group of seed plants. Flowering plants differ from them by having flowers and by growing fruits that wrap their seeds completely. Gymnosperms mostly rely on the wind to move their pollen. Flowering plants instead evolved nectar, bright colours and complex scents that draw in particular animal visitors.

paragraphs.heading: Partners with pollinators
paragraphs.text: Much of the group's success and quick spread into many species is credited to its long partnership with animal pollinators, above all insects, birds and bats. Over time, a flower's shape can come to match the body and senses of the animal that visits it most, a pattern called a pollination syndrome. Tube-shaped flowers, for instance, often evolve alongside hummingbirds or insects with long tongues. A small change in a flower's shape can switch a plant to a new pollinator, which can cut it off from its relatives and help give rise to new species.

paragraphs.heading: A late but fast rise
paragraphs.text: Fossil spores show that land plants have existed for at least 475 million years. The line leading to flowering plants split from the shared ancestor of today's gymnosperms over 300 million years ago, before the Carboniferous period ended. Yet flowering plants themselves appear suddenly in the Early Cretaceous, starting about 130 million years ago, far later than other major plant groups. Older claimed flower fossils are not widely accepted, since each can be explained as some other seed plant misidentified. During the Cretaceous they spread explosively and became the leading plants across the planet.

paragraphs.heading: Every size and habitat
paragraphs.text: With about 300,000 known species in 416 families, flowering plants are by far the most varied land plants. The tallest, Eucalyptus gum trees in Australia and Shorea faguetiana in Southeast Asian rainforests, can reach almost 100 metres. The smallest, Wolffia duckweeds, float on fresh water and measure under 2 millimetres across. About 99% feed themselves through photosynthesis, using sunlight to build molecules such as sugars, while the rest live as parasites on fungi or on other plants. They grow on land, in fresh water and in the sea, and they are the main plants in every land habitat except cold moss-lichen tundra and conifer forest.

paragraphs.heading: What people get from them
paragraphs.text: Farming depends almost wholly on flowering plants, and a handful of families supply nearly all plant food and animal feed. Rice, maize and wheat, all grasses in the family Poaceae, provide half of the staple calories eaten in the world. Other families give us wood, paper and cotton, along with ingredients for drinks, sugar, traditional remedies and modern medicines. People also grow flowers for decoration, and some flowers hold strong cultural meaning. Many species are now threatened by the destruction of their habitats and by climate change.
